content:
The water cycle, also known as the hydrologic cycle, describes the continuous movement of water on, above, and below Earth's surface through various processes. This natural phenomenon is critical for maintaining Earth's ecosystems and climate systems, representing one of the most important biogeochemical cycles on our planet.
 The cycle begins with evaporation, where solar energy transforms liquid water from oceans, lakes, rivers, and soil into water vapor. Oceans contribute approximately 86% of global evaporation, with the remaining 14% coming from terrestrial sources. A related process, transpiration, occurs when plants release water vapor through their leaves as part of photosynthesis and respiration. The combination of evaporation and transpiration is often referred to as evapotranspiration. The rate of evaporation depends on temperature, humidity, wind speed, and available solar energy, which explains why evaporation rates vary by season and geographic location.
 As water vapor rises into the atmosphere, it cools and undergoes condensation, forming tiny water droplets that aggregate into clouds. This phase change from gas to liquid releases latent heat, an important energy transfer mechanism in the atmosphere that influences weather patterns. Condensation occurs around condensation nucleiâtiny particles like dust, salt, or pollution that provide surfaces for water molecules to gather upon. The resulting cloud formations vary from low-lying stratus clouds to high-altitude cirrus clouds, each associated with different weather conditions.
 Water returns to Earth's surface through precipitation in the form of rain, snow, sleet, or hail when water droplets become too heavy to remain suspended in the air. Global precipitation averages about 1 meter annually but varies dramatically by region, from deserts receiving less than 25 cm to rainforests receiving over 400 cm per year. Precipitation that falls on land may follow several pathways: some infiltrates into the ground becoming groundwater, some flows across the surface as runoff eventually reaching streams and rivers, and some is intercepted by plants or human structures before reaching the ground.
 Groundwater moves much more slowly than surface water, with residence times ranging from days to thousands of years depending on the aquifer's properties. This underground water plays a crucial role in sustaining streamflow during dry periods and providing drinking water for human populations. Eventually, all water returns to large water bodies like oceans, where the cycle begins anew. This closed system means the amount of water on Earth remains relatively constant over time, though its distribution and form are continuously changing.

scenario.title: TerrAqua: Water Cycle Simulator
scenario.content: Students design and manage virtual terrariums that demonstrate the water cycle in closed ecosystems. The simulation visualizes water molecules changing states and moving through different pathways, with color-coding to track water movement. Students can adjust environmental factors like heat (solar radiation), terrarium shape (topography), plant density (transpiration rates), and soil types (infiltration rates) to observe how these variables affect cycle dynamics. The interactive display shows real-time measurements of water quantities in different reservoirs (air, plants, soil, surface pools) and flow rates between them. Challenge scenarios include creating specific environmental conditions like rainforests, deserts, or ocean-dominated systems.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Tracking Water's Journey Through Earth Systems
hypothesis.description: Students will be able to follow the step-by-step processes in the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection), identify factors that affect each phase transition, and explain the energy transformations that occur as water changes states in a closed system.
